It is important to recognize a limitation in the evidence. The student poll showed 72 votes for books and 48 for media, but only 120 of 600 students responded, and participation was voluntary. The results may not represent the whole school.

In conclusion, the books plan offers broader access, meets a documented need, and provides lasting value for every student at Riverton High. I think this is the best choice for our school.

Riverton High should spend its $6,000 grant on the books plan. While the creative media space offers real opportunities, the books plan meets a need students have already shown and reaches more of them, both at school and at home.

The evidence has limits. The poll favored books 72 to 48, but only 120 of 600 students responded voluntarily, so it reflects the students who chose to answer, not the whole school. Neither source shows how much either plan would improve learning.

Even with that uncertainty, the books plan offers wider, longer-lasting access, making it the stronger use of a one-time grant.

Riverton High should use its $6,000 grant for the creative media space. Both plans have value, but the media space gives students a resource many of them cannot get anywhere else.

According to Source B, the space would let students record podcasts, edit video, and work on presentations even if they lack the equipment at home. For a student without a computer or microphone, a video project is either impossible or much harder. The space would give those students the same starting point as classmates with better technology.

The space would also serve the whole school. Source B says the media club supports scheduled access for all students rather than priority for its members, and that students could learn from each other across subjects.

The strongest argument against this plan is about access. Sources A and C point out that books can be borrowed and used at home without internet, while the media equipment stays at school. That challenges my own reason, because the space helps students without resources only while they are in the building. However, books and recording equipment fill different gaps. A student who wants more books still has the current library, but a student without editing tools has no option at all. The six-seat limit is real, so the school should use the supervised booking system Source B describes.

The evidence also has limits. The 72-to-48 poll result came from only 120 of 600 students who chose to respond, and no source measures how much either plan would improve learning.

Because it closes a gap nothing else in the school addresses, the media space is the better investment.
